title: Lesson 1: What an Agent Actually Is (LLMs vs Rules vs Workflows)
description: The definitions that matter for the whole track: what separates a rules system, an LLM workflow, and a true agent, plus how to tell which one you're actually building.

questions.question: What single property best distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: The model, not your code, decides the path
The system includes at least one call to a language model
The system can handle more than one request per session
The system was assembled with a modern agent framework
questions.explanation: An agent is defined by who decides the path: the model directs its own process and tool use at runtime, while in a workflow your code fixes the path and the model only fills the steps.

questions.question: When the steps of a task can all be enumerated up front, why is a workflow usually the better choice than an agent?
options: It removes the need for any model calls at runtime
It guarantees the task can never fail
It is cheaper, faster, and easier to test
It requires no token budget to operate
questions.explanation: For a known path, agentic autonomy trades latency and cost for flexibility you will not use, so the simpler workflow is more reliable and cheaper.

questions.question: In an agent loop, what is the reliable way to confirm the goal has actually been met?
options: Trust the model's own confident assessment that it is done
Count how many iterations the loop has run
Add a deterministic gate that verifies the result
Check that the context window is not yet full
questions.explanation: The model's judgment that it is finished can be confidently wrong, so a deterministic external gate must verify the result before the loop declares success.
